sec.title: Background
sec.p: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has shown promise in overcoming resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in early-phase cancer trials. We investigated the safety, feasibility and efficacy of FMT from ICI responders to patients with advanced cancers progressing on ICIs.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This was a single-arm phase IIa basket trial (MITRIC; NCT05286294) including patients with ICI-refractory cancer. Long-term ICI responders were used as FMT donors. Patients received FMTs in combination with ICIs; two FMT administrations (by colonoscopy) were scheduled before the first radiological evaluation after 6 weeks, and up to three later FMTs were allowed (by enema). Co-primary endpoints were the evaluation of FMT-related adverse events and objective response rate. Feasibility, clinical benefit rate, progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), implant engraftment, immune response and biomarkers were among the secondary objectives.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The study enrolled 12 patients with melanoma (n=9), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; n=1), renal cell carcinoma (n=1) or microsatellite instability-high pancreatic cancer (n=1). FMT was well tolerated, whereas immune-related toxicity occurred in 6/12 patients. All patients received the first FMT; 10/12 patients also underwent the second FMT. No objective responses were observed, while 5/12 patients recorded stable disease. Clinical benefit per-protocol (stable disease >6 months) was achieved in a patient with melanoma, who had regression of some lesions and remains alive after 33 months without further systemic treatment. Mixed responses with regression of some lesions were observed in another melanoma patient, and in a patient with HNSCC. The median PFS was 1.5 months, and median OS was 10.1 months. Sequencing of fecal samples indicated engraftment after the first FMT in most patients. Mass cytometry analysis of peripheral blood cells suggested that an activated and differentiated T-cell signature was associated with improved PFS and OS, while a naïve T-cell phenotype and a myeloid-dominant environment were unfavorable. CD14+ monocytes and serum interleukin-8 increased at group level over time.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: FMT in combination with ICIs was safe and feasible in patients with advanced cancers, but with limited clinical activity. Further studies are required to clarify the potential benefit of FMT, identify the appropriate patient population and define criteria for donor selection.
Keywords: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor, Biomarker, Immune related adverse event - irAE, Immunotherapy

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Phase I/II single-arm studies in advanced melanoma and gastrointestinal cancer have reported that resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) may be overcome by fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). Applicability to other tumor types remains largely unexplored. Questions remain regarding patient and donor selection, and the FMT procedure.

This single-arm study evaluated FMTs in combination with ICIs to patients progressing on ICIs. No objective responses were seen in 12 patients with four different types of cancer. Clinical benefit was demonstrated in one patient, remaining alive without further systemic treatment, and mixed responses were observed in two more patients. FMT was well tolerated. An activated T-cell signature in blood was associated with improved outcomes, while a myeloid-dominant immune milieu was unfavorable and not counteracted by FMT.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: This study does not support FMT as a salvage therapy in a non-biomarker-driven population of advanced heavily pretreated patients progressing on ICIs. However, the study suggests that FMT can safely be combined with ICI in patients with advanced cancer and that some patients may derive a benefit.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized the treatment landscape in solid tumors and are now standard of care across multiple cancer types.1 ICI therapy may offer long-lasting clinical benefit in advanced disease, as demonstrated in melanoma.2 Nevertheless, ICI resistance is a challenge, and response rates across all cancers are estimated to be about 20%.3 Mechanisms of resistance to ICIs are multifaceted, comprising both tumor cell intrinsic and extrinsic factors, but often not possible to unravel in clinical routine.4 Resistance phenotypes include primary resistance, in which tumors do not respond to ICI therapy, and secondary resistance, which implies tumor progression after initial clinical benefit.5

The gut microbiota is considered a tumor-extrinsic factor influencing both ICI efficacy6,10 and toxicity,11 and is investigated as a potential biomarker in cancer immunotherapy.12 Several studies have identified taxa associated with response and resistance to ICIs, but generalizability across different studies has proven difficult.13,15 Further, therapeutic modulations of the gut microbiota are explored, with the aim of enhancing efficacy and improving outcomes.16 17 Pioneering clinical trials in melanoma have demonstrated that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is safe and suggested that a subset of patients with ICI refractory disease may respond after FMT.18 19 FMT has also been reported to reverse anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) resistance in gastrointestinal cancers.20

Although these early clinical data are promising, the actual benefit of FMT in immuno-oncology is unclear and questions remain about patient selection, choice of ICI backbone, optimal methods of FMT administration and feasibility across different types of cancer.21 None of the aforementioned trials included treatment with anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) antibodies. To further address these questions, we designed a single-arm basket trial (MITRIC; NCT05286294) evaluating safety and efficacy of repeated FMTs in patients with ICI refractory disease. The hypothesis was that microbiota modulation by FMT could overcome resistance to ICIs. Here, we report the clinical outcomes as well as translational studies elucidating biomarkers, microbiota engraftment and immunological effects.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: The MITRIC trial was a single-arm, phase IIa study evaluating the safety, feasibility and efficacy of FMT to patients with cancer with progressive disease on ICI therapy. The study included multiple cancer types, selected based on eligibility for standard ICI therapy and relatively high response rates: Metastatic melanoma, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; with >20% programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression), clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), non-small cell lung cancer (>20% PD-L1 expression) and microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H)/mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) solid cancers.

The key eligibility criteria included disease progression on ICIs, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0–1 and measurable disease according to immunotherapy Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (iRECIST). Prior response to ICIs was allowed, but with disease-specific criteria for the maximum time interval since progression on ICIs. For patients with melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer and MSI-H/dMMR cancer that had received subsequent lines of therapy after ICIs, re-introduction of ICIs and new disease progression was required. Study protocol and statistical analysis plan are available as online supplemental data files.
A Safety Monitoring Committee (SMC) oversaw the safety data during the study. The SMC consisted of two independent medical oncologists and one infectious disease physician.

sec.title: FMT donors and processing of FMT
sec.p: Key eligibility criteria for FMT donors were a cancer diagnosis and >12 months response to ICIs. Donors underwent safety screening by microbiological analyses of stool, blood and urine. The testing panel was developed by an expert group at Oslo University Hospital and based on international guidelines.22 During the stool delivery period, clinical assessment, microbiological testing and a screening questionnaire were performed every 6–12th week. Fresh feces were donated at the hospital and immediately processed by study personnel. On each donation day, a questionnaire was completed by donors to evaluate events that could harm the FMT products. Each processed FMT treatment consisted of 60 g feces suspended in 120 mL saline and 25 mL glycerol, which made a total FMT volume of 195 mL (±10 mL). The suspension was drawn on four syringes and stored at −80°C.

sec.title: Study interventions
sec.p: FMT was considered experimental but was not classified as a drug according to the Norwegian Medicines Agency. ICIs were not considered experimental.

The patients received FMT treatment until intolerable toxicity, disease progression (PD) per iRECIST or until the end of the intervention period. Up to five FMT administrations were allowed. The first two FMTs were given by colonoscopy with an interval of 4 weeks (week 1 and week 5, ±7 days). The 3rd–5th FMTs were delivered by enema (week 14, week 30, week 78). Each recipient only received FMT from a single donor. Before the procedure, patients underwent a standard bowel lavage. Antibiotics pretreatment prior to FMT was not given. FMT preparations were thawed in a water bath (37°C) before administration. In the case of colonoscopic administration, 100 mL fecal suspension was delivered in the terminal ileum and 100 mL fecal suspension in the cecum or installed as proximal in the colon as one could reach colonoscopically. Study biopsies were taken from the ileum, ascending colon and sigmoid colon. The administration of enema is comparable to a standard rectal contrast procedure for radiologic examination of the colon.23

The ICI treatment was kept unchanged from when progressive disease was recorded, and continued until PD per iRECIST, intolerable toxicity, or up to 2 years. If the patient had received combination therapy with anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-1 prior to study enrollment, a discussion in the study team determined whether monotherapy (anti-PD-1) or combination therapy was applied.

sec.title: Stool collection and 16S rRNA gene sequencing
sec.p: Fecal samples were collected in sterile containers at the hospital with immediate freezing at −80°C. For two patients, fecal samples were collected at home and stored at −20°C before transportation in a frozen condition to the hospital with storage at −80°C. Samples were shipped to Germany (Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology, Christian-Albrechts-University of Kiel) on dry ice for DNA extraction and sequencing. DNA extraction, 16S (V3-V4) sequencing and bioinformatics were performed as previously described.24 25 Engraftment of FMT was assessed by beta diversity analysis, through measuring the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between recipients and their respective donors across different time points.

sec.title: Mass cytometry and cytokine analyses
sec.p: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated using LymphoPrep density-gradient centrifugation (Abbott Rapid Diagnostics, Norway) and cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen until use. Frozen PBMCs were thawed at 37°C and processed for mass cytometry and acquired on a Helios cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) system as described previously.26 After bead normalization and debarcoding, the .fcs files were subjected to further clean-up (eg, removal of doublets, dead cells, debris, and beads) in FlowJo (V.10.8.1, FlowJo, Oregon, USA). The datasets were batch-corrected (cyCombine) and analyzed using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) and PhenoGraph in R (V.4.4.2). Manual gating was performed in FlowJo.

Serum cytokine profiling was performed using the Bio-Plex Pro Human Cytokine 27-plex assay (Bio-Rad Laboratories AS, Denmark), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Quantification was done as previously described.27 Only patients with available baseline samples were included. Proteins below the detection limit in baseline samples from all patients were excluded from the analysis. Interleukin (IL)-12 was below the detection limit in all patients except one, and was also excluded. Values below the detection limit were imputed by single value imputation, in which missing observations were replaced with the lowest measured value for that protein/sqrt(2).

sec.title: Study endpoints and statistics
sec.p: The co-primary endpoints were safety of FMT in patients with advanced cancer and tumor response evaluation by objective tumor response (ORR). ORR was defined as the proportion of patients with an objective tumor response (either partial response or complete response per investigator). Safety was assessed by the incidence, nature, and severity of adverse events (AE) according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI CTCAE), V.5.0. Secondary efficacy outcome measures were overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), durable response rate, clinical benefit rate and duration of objective response. Other secondary endpoints included feasibility of FMT for patients with advanced cancer measured as the percentage of patients receiving two FMTs, implant engraftment estimation, immune response and biomarkers.

Tumor response evaluation was assessed by iRECIST as the primary method28 and RECIST V.1.1 as the secondary method.29 After screening tumor assessments, evaluation of tumor response was performed every 6th week the first 3 months, every 8th week the next 9 months, and every 12th week thereafter.

All enrolled patients were included in the full analysis set (FAS), applied for the safety analyses and the primary efficacy outcome. Secondary outcome analyses were also performed both on FAS and on patients evaluable per-protocol, that is, patients that have received at least two doses of FMT.

PFS was defined as the time from enrollment to disease progression or death. OS was defined as the time from enrollment to death from any cause. Patients who were alive at the data cut-off were censored at the date of the last registered survival follow-up. Survival curves were calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method and p values were calculated using the log-rank method. The reverse Kaplan-Meier method was applied to estimate the median follow-up time.

Univariate Cox regression (HRs with 95% CIs) was used to assess how mass cytometry data and serum cytokines were associated with PFS and OS. Logistic regression was applied to evaluate predictors of immune-related adverse events (irAEs). Fold-change analyses were performed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Due to the exploratory nature of the analysis and the small sample size, no multiple-testing correction was applied.
Statistical analyses were performed in R V.4.4.0.30 All p values given are two-sided. P values<0.05 were considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Patient and donor characteristics
sec.p: According to the protocol, up to 20 patients were to be included in the study. Due to slow accrual, the trial was terminated after enrollment of 12 patients. Between June 2022 and January 2025, the study included 12 recipients with melanoma (n=9), ccRCC (n=1), HNSCC (n=1) or MSI-H pancreatic cancer (n=1). The baseline patient characteristics are summarized in online supplemental table S1. Median age was 64.5 years (50–79) and 10/12 were male. 50% had elevated baseline lactate dehydrogenase. All patients had metastatic disease and had progressed on ICI therapy in the metastatic setting, with ongoing disease progression at the time of enrollment. The cohort included patients with both primary and secondary ICI resistance; seven patients had no prior response to ICIs, three had a previous response, and two had a previous mixed response with regression of some lesions and progression of others.

Three male FMT donors were recruited, with a median age of 60 years. Two had been treated for metastatic melanoma and one for inoperable locally advanced cSCC. The donors had achieved long-term responses (range: 31–90 months) to ICIs (anti-PD-1 or anti-CTLA-4). All had ongoing partial (n=1) or complete (n=2) responses. Donor characteristics are described in online supplemental table S2.

sec.title: Feasibility and exposure of study interventions
sec.p: The study allowed for up to five sequential FMTs (figure 1A), administered by colonoscopy (first two FMTs) or enema (3rd–5th FMT). All enrolled patients received the first FMT. 10 out of 12 patients also underwent the second FMT (after 4 weeks). Feasibility, as measured by the percentage of patients receiving two FMTs, was a secondary trial endpoint. The study thus indicated that FMT treatment by colonoscopy is feasible in the studied population of patients with advanced cancer. In 2/12 patients, the second FMT was not performed due to rapid clinical deterioration or immune-related colitis. Four patients received a third FMT by enema (week 14). Due to disease progression, no patient received more than three FMTs.

sec.p: Prior to study enrollment, 3 out of the 12 patients had received subsequent anticancer therapies (chemotherapy, BRAF/MEK inhibitors) after progression on ICIs, and ICIs were consequently reintroduced in the study. The remaining nine patients had not received systemic therapy following progression on ICIs. In the study, nine patients received PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in monotherapy, while three patients received PD-1 and CTLA-4 inhibitors in combination. Type and dosage of ICIs were dependent on cancer form and included nivolumab monotherapy (480 mg flat dose every 4 weeks), pembrolizumab monotherapy (200 mg flat dose every 3 weeks (q3w)), atezolizumab monotherapy (1,200 mg flat dose q3w) or nivolumab plus ipilimumab (at 3 mg/kg q3w or 1 mg/kg q3w). The median cycles of ICIs in the study were 3.5 (range 1–7). The ICI therapy either continued according to the schedule as per study enrollment or was reintroduced shortly after the first FMT. The median time from the first FMT to ICI treatment was 5 days (range 2–14 days). At the time of data cut-off (September 19, 2025), all patients had discontinued FMTs and ICI treatment. Median follow-up time was 16.7 months (range 2.2–33.0).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: The evaluation of FMT-related AEs in patients with advanced cancer was a primary study endpoint. FMT was generally well tolerated. One patient experienced a grade 3 AE possibly related to the FMT procedure, with lower gastrointestinal bleeding a few days after colonoscopic study biopsies. Three more patients had FMT-related events, all of grade 1 and from the gastrointestinal tract. irAEs were registered in six patients (50%), mostly grade 1–2. In five of these six patients, irAEs had also been recorded prior to study enrollment. No grade 5 events were recorded. Table 2 summarizes AEs related to FMT and ICI treatment. A list containing all AEs is found in online supplemental table S3.

sec.title: Clinical activity of interventions
sec.p: The primary efficacy endpoint was ORR according to iRECIST. No objective responses were recorded (0/12). Five patients had stable disease as best overall response, while seven patients had PD as best response. Response data of individual patients are shown in figure 1B. The median PFS was 1.5 months, and median OS was 10.1 months (intention-to-treat population; online supplemental figure S1). Four patients were alive at data cut-off. The number of FMTs, PFS and OS of individual patients are displayed in figure 1C.

In one patient, we documented clinical benefit according to protocol criteria (secondary endpoint). This patient (recipient 3, melanoma) had a history of prior response before PD. In the study, the patient had initial disappearance of small non-target lung lesions. Recurrent immune-related hepatitis (grade 2) eventually led to discontinuation of anti-PD-1 therapy. Slow growth of target disease thereafter caused PD, after 6.4 months. After leaving the study, the recipient received palliative radiation therapy. Intriguingly, regression of non-radiated lesions was subsequently observed, consistent with an abscopal effect. The patient is alive at data cut-off (33 months after enrollment), and has not received any systemic treatment after the discontinuation of anti-PD-1 therapy in MITRIC.

Clinical activity with regression of some lesions was also observed in recipient 6 (melanoma), who had received ipilimumab plus nivolumab prior to study entry without clinical response or irAEs, followed by temozolomide. In the study, ipilimumab plus nivolumab was reintroduced shortly after the first FMT. The patient then developed immune-related colitis grade 2 and only received one FMT. At the initial radiological evaluation, growth of target lesions was observed (leading to unconfirmed progressive disease (iUPD)), but with regression of non-target lesions in bone and lymph nodes. At the second radiological assessment even the target lesions regressed. However, new lesions caused immune confirmed progressive disease (iCPD) per iRECIST and the patient left the study. The patient went on to receive additional ICI therapy, but passed away after 9.1 months.

We also enrolled patients with HNSCC, RCC or MSI-H pancreatic cancer. The patient with HNSCC had stable disease lasting until week 20, with some evidence of clinical activity. Prior to study enrollment, the patient had progressed on several treatment lines in the metastatic setting; (1) pembrolizumab (mixed response, before unequivocal progression) (2) cetuximab (PD) (3) re-introduction of pembrolizumab (PD). The first radiologic evaluation in the study showed mixed response with reduced size of a target lesion (lymph node; stable disease by iRECIST). At the second radiologic evaluation, another lymph node lesion was slightly reduced. However, at the third imaging iUPD was assigned based on new lesions and increase in non-target lesions, though other lesions were further regressed. The patient subsequently received palliative chemotherapy and is alive at data cut-off (16 months after enrollment). The patient with RCC experienced stable disease until week 14, while the patient with MSI-H pancreatic cancer had PD after 6 weeks (figure 1C).

sec.title: Engraftment of FMT
sec.p: Fecal samples from recipients were collected at baseline, 1 week after first FMT (week 2), prior to second FMT (week 5), and at later time points if feasible. Repeated fecal samples were collected from 11 of 12 recipients, in which evaluation of engraftment was achievable. All available fecal samples underwent 16S rRNA sequencing (n=40).

Beta diversity analysis was used to assess engraftment following FMT, with Bray-Curtis distance metrics applied to estimate the similarity between recipients and donors prior to FMT and at different time points. In 8 out of 10 recipients with available fecal samples at week 2, the similarity to corresponding donors increased 1 week after the first fecal transplant (paired Wilcoxon, p=0.049). However, in many recipients, the similarity to donors later decreased (figure 2A). The second or third FMT did not seem to lead to increased recipient-donor similarity, but due to few fecal samples, this was infeasible to determine. The exemption was recipient 3 (clinical benefit) who shifted away from the donor after the first FMT, but moved towards the donor after the second and third transplant and appeared to achieve durable engraftment.

sec.p: The alpha diversity varied among the donors, with a range comparable to the 11 recipients measured at baseline (figure 2B). We noticed that increased recipient-donor similarity after FMTs seemed to be associated with increased alpha diversity, and vice versa, across the sampled time points (online supplemental figure S2). Among the eight patients with increased recipient-donor similarity at week 2, seven had increased alpha diversity.

sec.title: Mass cytometry analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells
sec.p: We performed mass cytometry analysis on PBMCs collected at three time points to assess how immune cell subsets related to clinical outcomes, and to evaluate immunological changes following FMT and ICI therapy. The single-cell data from mass cytometry were subjected to dimensionality reduction using UMAP followed by Phenograph clustering, which led to the identification of 18 distinct immune cell populations (online supplemental figure S3). We first investigated treatment-induced changes and found that the abundance of different immune cell populations was largely stable between baseline and week 5. However, CD14+ monocytes were increased and CD56+ CD16⁻ natural killer cells decreased from baseline to later time points (online supplemental figure S4).

Next, we investigated associations between the identified immune cell types and PFS/OS. At baseline, a highly differentiated T-cell environment was related to improved PFS and OS, with CD8+ effector memory (EM) T cells and CD8+ terminally differentiated effector memory T cells re-expressing CD45RA (TEMRA) showing positive associations with favorable outcomes (figure 3A,B). In contrast, a myeloid skewed environment and a naïve T-cell phenotype appeared to be associated with poorer outcomes (figure 3A,B). The patient with clinical benefit had the lowest levels of CD14+ monocytes and highest levels of CD4+ EM among all 12 patients at baseline (online supplemental figure S5A). After 4 weeks of study treatment, CD14+ monocytes were significantly associated with increased hazard of progression and death, while CD4+ EM phenotype was associated with improved OS (figure 3A,B). At group level, patients with clinical benefit/mixed response had higher levels of CD4+EM cells at week 5 than the other patients (online supplemental figure S5B). A more detailed analysis of T-cell phenotypes within the CD4 and CD8 compartments suggested that granzyme B+ CD8+ T cells were associated with favorable outcomes, while ICOS+ CD8 T cells and Th2 cell levels were related to poorer prognosis (online supplemental figure S6A,B).

sec.p: We furthermore attempted to explore if these associations were related to the FMT intervention. This question cannot be concluded on without a control group. However, to inform on the question, we repeated the OS analyses for each immune cell subset using the initiation of ICI therapy in the metastatic setting as the start date, instead of study enrollment. Overall, we observed similar associations as described above. This exploratory analysis thus suggested that the observed associations between immune cell subsets and outcomes mainly reflected the patients’ disease and responsiveness to immunotherapy, rather than their response to FMT (online supplemental figure S6C and online supplemental figure S7).

Moreover, we investigated if immune cell subsets were associated with irAEs. A principal component analysis revealed a partial separation between patients with and without irAEs (figure 4A). Specifically, higher levels of regulatory T cells (Tregs), CD4+ EM, Th1 and ICOS+ CD8 T cells at baseline were associated with increased risk of developing irAEs (figure 4B,C).

sec.title: Serum cytokine profiling
sec.p: Serum cytokines were measured at baseline and week 5. The results showed an increase in most cytokines during the first 4 weeks, with IL-8 exhibiting the most significant increase followed by interferon-gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10) (figure 5A). In general, higher baseline cytokine levels tended to be associated with prolonged OS and PFS (OS: HR <1 for 18/19 cytokines; PFS: HR <1 for 16/19 cytokines) (figure 5B,C). RANTES and IL-4 were significantly associated with improved OS (unadjusted p values; figure 5C), while basic fibroblast growth factor (FGF basic) was borderline significant (p=0.06). None of the cytokines showed a significant association with PFS (figure 5B), or with the incidence of irAEs (online supplemental figure S8A). We finally repeated the OS analyses for each cytokine using the initiation of ICI therapy in the metastatic setting as the start date, instead of study enrollment. Again, higher baseline cytokine levels tended to be associated with prolonged OS (HR <1 for 16/19 cytokines). FGF basic was the only cytokine significantly associated with improved OS (online supplemental figure S8B).

caption.title: Serum cytokine changes during treatment and associations with clinical outcome. (A) Paired comparison of serum cytokine levels between pretreatment and week-5 samples, shown as log₂ fold change. Each point represents an individual patient. P values were computed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Cytokines with significant changes (p<0.05) are indicated with an asterisk. (B–C) Cox proportional hazards regression evaluating baseline cytokine concentrations and their association with (B) progression-free survival and (C) OS. HRs with 95% CIs are shown. HR >1 indicates increased risk, while HR <1 indicates reduced risk. Statistically significant associations (p<0.05) are annotated with an asterisk. n=11. PFS, progression-free survival; OS, overall survival.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, FMT from ICI responders was used to assess if gut microbiota modulation could overcome established ICI resistance in different cancer types. All patients had progressed on ICIs in the metastatic setting. We found that the study interventions had an acceptable safety profile, and that FMT was feasible in patients with advanced cancer, but observed no objective responses. A patient with melanoma had clinical benefit as defined in the protocol, with stable disease lasting more than 6 months, and remains alive after 33 months. Another patient with melanoma, who had no prior response or toxicity to ICIs, developed both evidence of response and immune-related toxicity, but eventually progressed and died. There has to our knowledge been no previous reports on FMT in HNSCC. In our trial, the patient with HNSCC had stable disease for 20 weeks and remains alive after 16 months.

The potential risk of transmission of infectious agents is a concern with FMT.31 However, FMT has for decades been used for Clostridioides difficile infections, and the available data indicate that most FMT-related AEs are low-grade and self-limiting.32 Previous trials have indicated that FMT is safe also in patients with cancer,18,2033 and the results from our trial, MITRIC, support the safety of FMT in patients with advanced cancer. All AEs related to FMT treatment were grade 1, while one grade 3 event was recorded following colonoscopy. IrAEs occurred in 50% of patients and were mostly mild. Five out of six patients with irAEs in MITRIC had also experienced irAEs prior to study enrollment, suggesting that FMT did not increase the risk of irAEs. We furthermore found that irAEs were related to higher baseline PBMC levels of differentiated CD4+T cells with an EM and Th1 phenotype, as well as Tregs and ICOS+ CD8 T cells. This observation suggests that a pre-existing activated immune milieu may predispose to irAEs. However, from our dataset, it cannot be determined whether this phenotype was induced by prior ICI exposure.

Previous single-arm studies have reported a potential for FMT to reverse ICI resistance. Two proof-of-concept trials in metastatic melanoma demonstrated clinical benefit in patients with anti-PD-1-refractory disease: Baruch et al19 reported objective responses in 3 of 10 patients, and Davar et al18 reported responses in 3 of 15 patients, with durable stable disease in three additional patients. Kim et al20 observed objective responses in 1 of 13 patients with upper gastrointestinal cancers progressing on PD-1 inhibition. FMT combined with ICIs is also being evaluated in the first-line setting. Recently, several single-arm studies have evaluated healthy-donor FMT in combination with anti-PD-1 monotherapy or anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4 therapy as first-line treatment in advanced melanoma,36 37 advanced non-small cell lung cancer36 and metastatic RCC.34 These studies suggest that FMT may enhance the efficacy of ICIs in the treatment-naïve setting. In addition, results from the randomized TACITO trial were recently published,35 indicating potential clinical activity of FMT combined with first-line anti-PD-1 therapy and a tyrosine kinase inhibitor in metastatic RCC, using ICI responders as donors.

Various factors may explain the discrepancy between encouraging findings from previous FMT studies and the absence of confirmed responses in MITRIC. First, the small sample size represents an important limitation, as in earlier FMT trials conducted in ICI-resistant disease. Second, heterogeneity across studies—including differences in donor selection, FMT preparation, route of administration, and treatment schedule—may influence clinical and biological outcomes. Patient selection is also likely critical. In the studies by Baruch et al, Davar et al, and Kim et al, most responses occurred relatively late and were sometimes preceded by pseudo-progression, suggesting that patients with rapidly progressive disease and short expected survival may not be optimal candidates.18,20 In MITRIC, most patients presented with disseminated, fast-growing disease, which may not have allowed sufficient time for FMT to exert meaningful effects. We included both patients with and without previous ICI benefit, and it remains unclear in which clinical context microbiota modulation is most relevant. The recently accumulating first-line evidence,34 36 37 including randomized data,35 raises the possibility that the ICI-naïve setting may be better suited for FMT strategies. Donor characteristics are also likely crucial. As in other trials of ICI-refractory disease, we used long-term ICI responders as stool donors; however, microbial composition varies considerably among such donors, and it is unknown whether this approach is superior to using healthy donors. The small number of available donors adds uncertainty. Notably, all responders in Baruch et al received stool from a single donor,19 whereas our study used three donors, raising the possibility of suboptimal donor-recipient matching or lack of specific microbial communities required for benefit. Donor age may also influence microbial diversity, although older donors were likewise used in Davar et al.18 Finally, microbiota composition is shaped by diet, geography, medications, and host factors, contributing to inconsistent “beneficial” signatures across studies.13 14 Thus, FMT may be effective only in selected populations, and the gut microbiota represents just one of several determinants of immunotherapy outcome; reliable biomarkers to identify patients most likely to benefit from microbiota modulation have not yet been established.

The MITRIC trial used repeated FMT treatments, under the premise that this should increase engraftment and thus the possibility of clinical success. The gut microbiota in most recipients shifted towards their respective donors 1 week after the first FMT, but this effect seemed transient in most recipients. As the patients progressed, it was not feasible to collect stool samples at later time points to assess long-term engraftment and the effects of repeated FMTs. One patient had long-term engraftment and, intriguingly, this was the only patient with clinical benefit in the study. This is in line with FMT studies in melanoma that have suggested long-term donor-recipient similarities only in responders.33

The PBMC data suggest that in this patient population, a highly differentiated T-cell environment is associated with improved PFS and OS, while a myeloid skewed and Th2-like environment suggests a poor prognosis. These findings are in line with existing knowledge on cancer immunity,4 38 and may reflect that these patients are treated with ICIs, which relies on the host immune response for their efficacy. The OS times calculated from the start of ICI therapy support that these observations represent immunological characteristics prognostic for patients treated with ICIs, and are not related to the FMT intervention. In particular, granzyme B+ CD8+ T cells were associated with favorable outcomes. Using the same mass cytometry panel, we recently identified this particular subset to be associated with clinical benefit from ICIs in a randomized breast cancer study.26

The FMT in MITRIC did not appear to induce changes in the systemic immune milieu, as measured by peripheral PBMC phenotypes. It would be of interest to explore if other FMT protocols or microbiota interventions could alter the PBMC signatures, and if this is related to clinical efficacy from FMT. Davar et al found that the clinical responders exhibited higher levels of CD56+CD8+ T cells in PBMCs after FMT/anti-PD-1 treatment, and that this subset expressed higher levels of various activation markers.18 Furthermore, Davar et al reported that responding patients had decreased circulating IL-8 and decreased frequencies of IL-8-producing myeloid cells in tumors. In contrast, we observed an increase in CD14+ monocytes and IL-8 during the study. Moreover, higher CD14+ monocyte levels after 4 weeks were in MITRIC associated with shorter PFS and OS. It is possible that increasing myeloid-driven immunosuppression in our patients during the course of the trial was related to the lack of benefit from FMT. However, the exploratory PBMC and cytokine data were not corrected for multiple testing in this study, and these findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited sample size.

In conclusion, the MITRIC trial demonstrated that FMT in combination with ICIs is safe and feasible in patients with advanced cancers. While indications of clinical activity were observed in a few patients, FMT did not result in objective clinical responses in patients refractory to ICIs. Further research is needed to clarify whether FMT can enhance ICI efficacy, optimize FMT protocols, and establish criteria for donor and recipient selection.
